procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated the 23rd May, 1953, of the Election Tribunal, Himachal Pradesh, Simla, in Election Petition No. 14 of 1952 dismissing the petition.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There was no High Court proceeding. The Election Tribunal is the court of first instance for election petitions.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appeal by Special Leave granted by the Supreme Court on the 25th January, 1954.

issue.issue_text: Whether the disqualifications laid down in Section 7 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Act XLIII of 1951) apply to elections held in Part C States under the Government of Part C States Act, 1951 (Act XLIX of 1951), by virtue of Section 17 of the latter Act.

facts: The case concerned an election held in a Part C State, which was governed by the Government of Part C States Act, 1951 (Act XLIX).
The central issue was whether the disqualifications for candidates listed in Section 7 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Act XLIII) applied to these elections.

This question arose because Section 17 of the Part C States Act (Act XLIX) incorporates disqualifications for Parliament, while Section 8 of the same Act explicitly omits the part of the Representation of the People Act (Part II) that contains Section 7.

law.name: Section 17 of the Government of Part C States Act, 1951 (Act XLIX)
law.description: A person is disqualified from being a member of a Part C State's Legislative Assembly if they are disqualified from being a member of either House of Parliament under the provisions of Article 102 of the Constitution.

law.name: Article 102(1)(e) of the Constitution
law.description: This article states that a person shall be disqualified for being chosen as a member of either House of Parliament if they are disqualified by or under any law made by Parliament.

law.name: Section 7 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Act XLIII)
law.description: This section, located in Part II of the Act, is a law made by Parliament under Article 102(1)(e) that lists specific disqualifications for membership in Parliament.

law.name: Section 8 of the Government of Part C States Act, 1951 (Act XLIX)
law.description: This section applies Parts I and III to XI of the Representation of the People Act (Act XLIII) to elections in Part C States, but it notably omits Part II, which contains Section 7.

application.point: The Court first addressed the argument that since Act XLIII did not apply on its own (proprio vigore) to Part C States, a candidate was not technically disqualified 'by or under' that law.
application.reasoning: The Court rejected this by analyzing the specific wording of Section 17 of Act XLIX. It held that the section creates a hypothetical test: if a person *would be* disqualified to be chosen for Parliament under a law like Act XLIII, they are then disqualified for the State Assembly. The key is not whether Act XLIII applies directly, but whether the conditions for disqualification under it are met.

application.point: The Court then considered the main argument: that the deliberate omission of Part II (containing Section 7) from the list of applicable sections in Section 8 of Act XLIX showed a clear legislative intent to exclude those disqualifications.
application.reasoning: The Court refuted this by examining the 'general scheme' of the Part C States Act (Act XLIX). It reasoned that the framers of this Act intended to create a comprehensive election code. They dealt with the subject of qualifications and disqualifications (the subject of Part II of Act XLIII) in their own specific provisions, namely Sections 7 and 17 of Act XLIX. Since Act XLIX already covered this ground, there was no need to also extend Part II of Act XLIII via Section 8. Therefore, the omission in Section 8 was not an intentional exclusion but a result of the subject being handled elsewhere in the Act.

application.point: The Court found no conflict between Section 8 and Section 17.
application.reasoning: It concluded that Section 8 'passively omits' Part II because its subject matter is covered elsewhere, while Section 17 'positively enacts' that the disqualifications for Parliament (which are found in Section 7 of Act XLIII) are to be applied. To accept the respondent's argument would render the reference in Section 17 to parliamentary disqualifications meaningless.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the disqualifications laid down in Section 7 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Act XLIII) must be held to be comprised within Section 17 of the Government of Part C States Act, 1951 (Act XLIX). Consequently, these disqualifications do apply to elections held in Part C States.

issue.issue_text: Whether the omission of Part II (which contains Section 7) of Act XLIII of 1951 in Section 8 of Act XLIX of 1951 indicates a legislative intent to exclude those disqualifications from applying to elections in Part C States.

facts: Act XLIX of 1951 was enacted to govern elections in Part C States.
Section 8 of this Act explicitly applied Parts I and III through XI of an earlier law, Act XLIII of 1951, to these elections.
Notably, Section 8 omitted any mention of Part II of Act XLIII of 1951.
Part II of Act XLIII of 1951 contains Section 7, which lists various disqualifications for candidates.
The argument was made that because Part II was deliberately omitted from Section 8, the disqualifications in Section 7 were not intended to apply to elections in Part C States.
law: Section 17 of Act XLIX of 1951 states that a person is disqualified from being chosen for a State Assembly if they would be disqualified from being chosen as a member of either House of Parliament.
Section 7 of Act XLIII of 1951 lists disqualifications for being chosen as a member of Parliament.
application: The Court rejected the argument by examining the overall legislative "scheme" of Act XLIX of 1951.
It determined that the framers of Act XLIX intended to create a comprehensive election code for Part C States, using Act XLIII as a model.

The Court found that the subject matter of Part II of the earlier act (qualifications and disqualifications) was not simply ignored, but was actively addressed by specific provisions within the new Act XLIX of 1951, namely its own Sections 7 and 17.
Since Act XLIX already had its own sections covering qualifications and disqualifications, there was no need to also incorporate Part II of the earlier act via Section 8.

The Court found no inconsistency between Section 8 and Section 17. It described the omission in Section 8 as a "passive" omission (because the topic was handled elsewhere), while Section 17 was a "positive" enactment that directly incorporated the parliamentary disqualifications.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the omission of Part II from Section 8 did not signify a legislative intent to exclude the disqualifications from Section 7 of Act XLIII of 1951. Instead, the overall scheme of the new Act showed that these disqualifications were intended to apply to Part C State elections through the separate mechanism of Section 17.

issue.issue_text: Whether contracts with the administration of a Part C State (Himachal Pradesh) are to be construed as contracts with the Central Government for the purposes of election disqualification.

facts: The case concerned an election to the Legislative Assembly of Himachal Pradesh, which was a Part C State.
The elected candidate, Sri Padam Dev, had contracts for the supply of goods.
The records showed that these contracts were with the Chief Commissioner, who was in charge of the administration of the State of Himachal Pradesh, not directly with the Central Government.
law: The appellant's argument was based on Article 239 of the Constitution, which states that Part C States shall be administered by the President.
The appellant connected this to Article 77, which provides that all executive action of the Government of India is taken in the name of the President.

The appellant's legal theory was that since the President is the executive head of both the Central Government and Part C States, any contract with a Part C State is, in law, a contract with the Central Government.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, calling the reasoning a "fallacy."

The Court clarified that when the President administers a Part C State under Article 239, he is not functioning as the executive head of the Central Government. Instead, he is acting as the head of that specific State, in a position analogous to a Governor in a Part A State.
The Court emphasized that although Part C States were centrally administered, they did not lose their legal identity as separate States or become merged with the Central Government.

To support this distinction, the Court pointed out that under Section 38(2) of the Government of Part C States Act, executive actions of the State were taken in the name of the Chief Commissioner, whereas executive actions of the Central Government are taken in the name of the President (Article 77). This difference in procedure highlights their separate legal existence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was no basis in law or on the facts to support the contention that contracts with the administration of a Part C State (Himachal Pradesh) are to be construed as contracts with the Central Government. The two were held to be legally distinct entities.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appointment of a Government servant as a polling agent, by itself, constitutes a corrupt practice under Section 123(8) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

facts: A candidate, Sri Padam Dev, appointed Sital Singh, an extra-departmental agent (a type of Government servant), as one of his polling agents.

law.law_text: Section 123(8) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, defines procuring the assistance of a Government servant for the furtherance of a candidate's election prospects as a corrupt practice.
There is nothing in the Representation of the People Act, 1951, or its associated Rules that explicitly bars the appointment of a Government servant as a polling agent.

The Court relied on its previous decision in Raj Krushna Bose v. Binod Kanugo, which held that a Government servant proposing or seconding a candidate was not a corrupt practice, applying the same reasoning to the role of a polling agent.

application.reasoning: The Court analyzed the specific duties of a polling agent, which are primarily to identify voters and ensure the secrecy of the voting process.
It reasoned that these duties, when properly performed, do not in themselves further the election prospects of the candidate. The act of identifying a voter is neutral.

The Court distinguished between the mere appointment and the actual conduct of the agent. While acknowledging that a Government servant's presence could potentially lead to unfair practices, it held that such improper conduct must be proven. The appointment itself is not inherently a corrupt act.
Therefore, as long as the Government servant, acting as a polling agent, confines themselves to their prescribed duties, Section 123(8) is not violated.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that, as an abstract proposition of law, the mere appointment of a Government servant as a polling agent is not, by itself and without more, a corrupt practice under Section 123(8) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

issue.issue_text: Whether the respondent was disqualified due to having a subsisting contract with the government at the material time.

facts: The respondent had contracts for the supply of goods with the Himachal Pradesh State Government.
Himachal Pradesh was a Part C State at the time.

The appellant contended that because Part C States are administered by the President under Article 239 of the Constitution, a contract with the State Government was legally a contract with the Central Government.
law: Disqualification for elections in Part C States was governed by Section 17 of Act No. XLIX of 1951.
Section 17 states that a person is disqualified for the State Assembly if they would be disqualified for being chosen to either House of Parliament.
The law for disqualification for Parliament (Section 7(d) of Act No. XLIII of 1951) specifies that the disqualifying contract must be with the 'appropriate Government'.
For elections to Parliament, the 'appropriate Government' is defined as the 'Central Government'.
application: The Court established that to be disqualified, the respondent must have had a contract with the Central Government.
The Court then examined whether the respondent's contracts with the Himachal Pradesh State Government could be considered contracts with the Central Government.

It rejected this argument, explaining that when the President administers a Part C State under Article 239, he functions as the head of that State, not as the executive head of the Central Government.

The Court concluded that the central administration of Part C States did not merge them with the Central Government. Therefore, the respondent's contracts were with the State Government, not the Central Government.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the claim that the respondent was disqualified. Since the respondent's contracts were with the Himachal Pradesh State Government and not the Central Government, he did not meet the legal criteria for disqualification for being elected to Parliament, and was therefore not disqualified for being elected to the State Legislative Assembly.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the disqualifications laid down in Section 7 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (Act XLIII of 1951) apply to elections held in Part C States under the Government of Part C States Act, 1951 (Act XLIX of 1951), by virtue of Section 17 of the latter Act.
appellant_arguments: The disqualifications laid down in Section 7 of Act XLIII of 1951, a law made by Parliament, fall under Article 102(1)(e) of the Constitution.
By virtue of Section 17 of Act XLIX of 1951, these disqualifications are attracted to elections held in Part C States.
respondent_arguments: Act XLIII of 1951 does not apply 'proprio vigore' (by its own force) to elections in Part C States.
Therefore, a candidate in a Part C State is not a person disqualified 'by or under the terms of that law' as required by Article 102(1)(e), and is not affected by Section 17.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the omission of Part II (which contains Section 7) of Act XLIII of 1951 in Section 8 of Act XLIX of 1951 indicates a legislative intent to exclude those disqualifications from applying to elections in Part C States.
appellant_arguments: The respondent's construction would give no meaning to the words 'disqualified for being chosen as a member of either House of Parliament' in Section 17.
No inference can be drawn from the non-inclusion of Section 7 in Section 8, as both sections can be given their full effect without conflict.
respondent_arguments: Section 8 of Act XLIX of 1951, which applies Parts I and III to XI of Act XLIII of 1951 to Part C State elections, deliberately omits Part II, which contains Section 7.
This omission by design shows a legislative intent that Section 7 should not apply to these elections.
To avoid inconsistency, Section 17 should be construed in a way that does not defeat this clear legislative intention.

arguments.issue_text: Whether contracts with the administration of a Part C State (Himachal Pradesh) are to be construed as contracts with the Central Government for the purposes of election disqualification.
appellant_arguments: Under Article 239 of the Constitution, Part C States are administered by the President.
Under Article 77, all executive action of the Government of India is in the name of the President.
Since the President is the executive head of both the Central Government and Part C States, contracts entered into with Part C States are, in law, contracts with the Central Government.
respondent_arguments: The disqualification under Section 7(d) applies only if a candidate has a contract with the 'appropriate Government', which for a Parliamentary election is the Central Government.
The contracts in question were with the administration of the Part C State of Himachal Pradesh, not the Central Government.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the respondent was disqualified due to having a subsisting contract with the government at the material time.
appellant_arguments: The Election Tribunal's statements of law regarding what constitutes a 'subsisting contract' were erroneous.
The Tribunal incorrectly held that a contract is not subsisting if goods have been delivered, even if the price remains payable, a view contrary to Supreme Court precedent.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's contracts with the government were not subsisting at the material dates. (This is the implied position upheld by the Election Tribunal).

cases.principle: A contract is considered to be subsisting if goods have been delivered thereunder but the price for them remains due and payable.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under Article 239 of the Constitution, the President administers a Part C State as the executive head of that State, not as the executive head of the Central Government. Consequently, a Part C State does not legally merge with the Central Government, and a contract entered into with a Part C State is not a contract with the Central Government.
obiter: The view that a contract is not subsisting if goods have been delivered but the price remains due is erroneous.

It is an anomaly that a contract with a State Government does not disqualify a candidate for the State Legislature in a Part C State, when such a contract would operate as a disqualification in other types of States.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Although the disqualifications for members of Parliament, as laid down in Section 7 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, are applicable to candidates in Part C State elections by virtue of Section 17 of the Government of Part C States Act, 1951, the respondent was not disqualified. This is because the contracts in question were with the administration of the Part C State of Himachal Pradesh, which is a distinct legal entity from the Central Government for the purposes of election law. Furthermore, the mere appointment of a government servant as a polling agent is not, by itself, a corrupt practice.
legal_tests_applied: Harmonious Construction of Statutes: When interpreting a statute, provisions should be read in a way that gives effect to all of them and avoids inconsistency or repugnancy. The court applied this to reconcile Section 8 and Section 17 of Act XLIX of 1951, concluding that the omission of Part II of Act XLIII in Section 8 did not nullify the import of its disqualifications through Section 17.

Constitutional Role Differentiation: The court analyzed the distinct constitutional capacities of a single authority (the President), holding that the President's function as the executive head of the Central Government is separate from the power to administer Part C States under Article 239. Action in one capacity does not equate to action in the other.

Per Se Illegality vs. Factual Violation: The court distinguished between an act that is illegal in and of itself (per se) and an act that becomes illegal only if accompanied by proven prohibited conduct. It determined that appointing a government servant as a polling agent falls into the latter category and is not a per se violation of election law.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that contracts with a Part C State are legally contracts with the Central Government was rejected as a 'fallacy'. The court reasoned that the President, when administering a Part C State under Article 239, is not functioning as the executive head of the Central Government but as the head of the State, and that Part C States do not cease to be distinct states or merge with the Central Government.

The appellant's claim that the mere appointment of a government servant as a polling agent constitutes a corrupt practice under Section 123(8) was dismissed. The court found nothing in the statute, rules, or the nature of a polling agent's duties (which is merely to identify voters) that would make such an appointment a violation 'by itself and without more'.

The appellant's argument that the omission of Part II of Act XLIII of 1951 from Section 8 of Act XLIX of 1951 signified a legislative intent to exclude its disqualifications was unsuccessful. The court held that such a construction would render the phrase 'disqualified for being chosen as a member of either House of Parliament' in Section 17 meaningless.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully established that the contracts triggering the disqualification claim were with the Himachal Pradesh State Government, not the Central Government. The court agreed that under Section 7(d) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, the 'appropriate Government' for a Parliamentary disqualification is the Central Government, and a contract with the State administration did not meet this criterion.

The court accepted the legal principle that the appointment of a government servant as a polling agent is not inherently a corrupt practice. The respondent prevailed on this point because the appellant did not prove any specific conduct by the agent that furthered the respondent's election prospects, relying only on the fact of the appointment itself.
policy_considerations: The court acknowledged the practical political concern that appointing a government servant as a polling agent 'might prove to be a source of unfair election practices'. However, it declined to create a blanket legal prohibition based on this potential risk, instead requiring that if such unfairness occurs, it must be factually established, thus balancing theoretical dangers against the need for concrete proof of wrongdoing.
